title: Hybridisation in Simple Molecules and Hydrocarbons

pages.title: Use orbital direction to explain a molecular shape

blocks.text: A straight BeCl₂ molecule, flat BF₃ and tetrahedral CH₄ require different arrangements of bonding orbitals. Hybridisation provides directed combinations of orbitals suitable for these patterns.
Begin with the number of electron domains and the bonding requirements. A hybridisation label should explain a known pattern, not replace electron counting or become a magic shape rule.

pages.transition: Check what orbital mixing changes and what it conserves.

pages.title: Understand the mixing conditions

blocks.text: Hybridisation combines atomic orbital functions of comparable energy on the same atom. The number of resulting hybrids equals the number of participating orbitals. Filled and half-filled orbitals can participate in appropriate descriptions.

Electron promotion is not an essential separate experimental event for every hybridised atom. Hybridisation is a mathematical bonding model, not a mechanical collision that blends physical orbitals like liquids.

pages.transition: Start with the simplest two-direction hybrid set.

pages.title: Construct linear sp hybrids

blocks.text: One s and one p orbital form two sp hybrids directed 180° apart. Each has 50% s character. Two unhybridised p orbitals remain available when the atom has a full valence s, p set.
The simple BeCl₂ molecular description uses two Be sp hybrids for two σ bonds. The sp label specifies the mixing count and resulting directions.

The exponent in sp² counts two p functions mixed with one s function; it does not mean two electrons or a 2+ ionic charge. The total is three input orbitals and therefore three hybrids. An unused p orbital can remain for π bonding.

pages.transition: Add another p orbital to obtain three planar directions.

pages.title: Construct trigonal planar sp² hybrids

blocks.text: One s and two p orbitals form three sp² hybrids, ideally 120° apart in a plane. Each has one-third s character. One p orbital remains perpendicular to the plane.
In BF₃, three hybrids describe three σ bonds around B. In an alkene carbon, the remaining unhybridised p orbital can participate in a π bond.

pages.transition: Four directions require one s plus three p functions.

pages.title: Construct tetrahedral sp³ hybrids

blocks.text: One s and three p orbitals form four sp³ hybrids, ideally 109.5° apart, each with 25% s character. CH₄ uses all four for σ bonds.
NH₃ and H₂O also have four electron domains, but lone pairs occupy some hybrid directions. Their molecular shapes become pyramidal and bent, with angles smaller than ideal tetrahedral values.

pages.transition: Apply the tetrahedral description to both carbon atoms in ethane.

pages.title: Explain every bond in ethane

blocks.text: Ethane is CH₃–CH₃. Each carbon uses an sp³ description: three hybrids overlap with H 1s orbitals, while one overlaps with the other carbon’s sp³ hybrid.
The molecule has six C–H σ bonds and one C–C σ bond: seven σ bonds and no π bond. Rotation about the C–C axis is possible because σ overlap can be retained.

pages.transition: A double bond requires a remaining p orbital for sideways overlap.

pages.title: Explain every bond in ethene

blocks.text: Ethene is CH₂=CH₂. Each carbon uses three sp² hybrids for two C–H σ bonds and one C–C σ bond. The remaining p orbitals are parallel and overlap sideways.
Ethene therefore has five σ bonds and one π bond. The planar arrangement allows π overlap; rotating one CH₂ unit out of alignment disrupts it and costs energy.

pages.transition: A triple bond needs two unhybridised p directions.

pages.title: Explain every bond in ethyne

blocks.text: Ethyne is HC≡CH. Each carbon uses two sp hybrids: one forms C–H σ overlap and one forms C–C σ overlap. Two unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon remain.
Two perpendicular sets of sideways p overlap make two π bonds. Thus ethyne has three σ and two π bonds, with a linear carbon-centred arrangement.

pages.transition: Compare the hybrid sets and the associated carbon-bond distances.

pages.title: Compare s character and bond lengths

blocks.text: The progression sp³, sp², sp has 25%, about 33.3%, and 50% s character. Greater s character holds hybrid electron density closer to the nucleus and contributes to shorter bonds in appropriate comparisons.
For related carbon bonds, increased multiplicity also shortens the C–C distance: ethane>ethene>ethyne. Explain which feature is changing rather than attributing every length difference to one factor.
For a linear HC≡N fragment, carbon needs two σ directions and two π components, fitting an sp description. Count the C–H and C–N σ links separately from the two π components of the triple bond.

pages.transition: Verify every atom’s directions and every σ/π component.

pages.title: Count domains, hybrids and unhybridised orbitals

blocks.text: Two, three and four hybrid directions correspond to sp, sp², sp³. Any unhybridised p orbitals may provide π overlap. Lone pairs count as domains but are not bonded atoms.
A useful check is to count σ and π components from connectivity, then verify that each atom has appropriate orbital directions. This links molecular structure to its bonding model.

questions.question: How many sp² hybrids form from one s and two p orbitals?
questions.answer: Three, with one unhybridised p orbital remaining in the valence set.

questions.question: Which hybrid set has 50% s character?
questions.answer: sp, because one of the two combined orbital functions is s.

questions.question: Count σ and π bonds in ethane.
Count σ and π bonds in ethene.
Why is ethyne linear at each carbon?
questions.answer: Its two sp hybrid directions are 180° apart.

questions.question: Do NH₃ and CH₄ have the same molecular shape?
questions.answer: No. Both have four domains, but NH₃ has a lone pair and is pyramidal.

questions.question: Does hybridisation change the number of orbitals?
questions.answer: No. Two, three or four input orbitals give the same number of hybrids.
